entry.title: Do ORCA simulations give us a richer training set?

link.title: Do ORCA simulations give us a richer training set?

entry.content:
What this post covers

My supervisor suggested a quantum-chemical descriptor strand, the argument for it is reasonable: a model trained on 2D structure has no access to electron density, and combining cheap quantum chemistry with machine learning has a real literature behind it.1 If frontier orbital energies or partial charges carry anything about CYP inhibition that a fingerprint does not, that is new information rather than a rearrangement of what I already have.

This post covers measuring the cost before committing to it, the full run and the problem it ran into, and then three independent attempts to show the descriptors are worth something: as features in a linear model, as a decorrelated ensemble member and inside the graph network itself. Every score below is a half-set measurement.2

The short version is that all three failed, and in two of the three the thing that produced the answer was a control I had added almost as an afterthought.

Measuring the machine instead of assuming it

Notebook 41 replaced the plan’s assumptions about the compounds with measurements, using RDKit3 over the SMILES already on disk. Two of the four answers came back differently from what the plan expected.

The size tail is not a problem. Heavy atom count has a median of 24 and a 99th percentile of 34, and exactly 3 of 5,655 compounds sit above 50 heavy atoms. The expensive compounds are a named handful, not a chemotype or an isoform.

Chirality is not merely deferred, it is unavailable. Of the 750 blind compounds, 266 carry at least one stereocentre and only 18 have every centre specified. Among blind compounds that have a centre at all, 93.2% carry an unassigned one. I checked whether my own curation had stripped the information by comparing four separate SMILES sources, from the raw challenge file through to the live featurisation code, and the counts are identical on every one. The information was never there. A chirality descriptor cannot be computed for the great majority of the compounds that are actually scored, so the sensitivity check I had been carrying since August is not pending, it is impossible.

The audit also found two smaller things worth recording. The logd_proxy column in my own feature set is bit-identical to logp on all 5,655 rows, so a nine-descriptor set has eight distinct values. And stereocenter_count, which I had been treating as a count of assigned configurations, counts potential centres whether specified or not.

Notebook 42 then measured the cost on fifteen compounds spanning the size range and the two chemotypes flagged as SCF risks, before committing to the full set. Conformers from RDKit’s ETKDG,4 then ORCA5,6 for a GFN2-xTB7 geometry optimisation followed by a B3LYP8,9-D310/def2-SV(P)11 single point.

The timing verdict was that the DFT single point averages 0.57 min at six cores across the population, under the 2-minute bar frozen before any of it ran, so the full set was viable at 166.8 h. The geometry step, not the DFT step, turned out to dominate at 66% of that.

Six fits were compared to decide which size measure predicts cost. Basis function count won on every metric, with the lowest leave-one-out error at 24.8%, and it won 69.9% of bootstrap resamples against a 70.0% bar frozen before any result was seen. The verdict reads NOT RESOLVED, and the notebook states that the bar is not moved to meet it. Nothing downstream would have changed if I had moved it.

The production run then went through: 5,655 compounds, 11,310 ORCA jobs, zero failures.

The atom that coordinates the iron

The most chemically motivated use of per-atom quantum data is the charge on whichever atom coordinates the haem iron. Notebook 43 tried to find that atom.

It also corrected a premise I had been working from. I had recorded Correia and Hollenberg12 as supporting computation on the neutral species. Read properly, “neutral” there qualifies the enzyme’s redox state, ferric against ferrous, not the ligand, and the passage concerns anions. Beck et al.13 point the other way for CYP2D6, describing substrates that procure a positive charge. The decision to compute neutral species stands, because 11,310 jobs rest on it, but its justification changed.

Three nested SMARTS definitions were measured over all 5,655 compounds. The conservative one, aliphatic basic nitrogen only, is the same pattern behind the CYP2D6 descriptor set from Kiani and Jabeen.14 The second adds aromatic nitrogen, which is what the cited chemistry actually describes. The third adds divalent sulfur and hydroxyl oxygen.

Definition Compounds matched CYP2D6 enrichment Empty on the blind set
Conservative, aliphatic basic N 17.9% 2.84× 88.4%
Faithful, plus aromatic N 79.0% 1.09× 23.1%
Inclusive, plus S and OH 84.6% 1.05× 18.3%

That is the bind, and it is not a matter of choosing more carefully between the three. The definition faithful to the chemistry matches four compounds in five and selects an atom in nearly all of them, so it carries almost no information. The definition that selects is empty for 88.4% of the compounds I am actually scored on. Worse for the idea, the mere presence flag of the conservative pattern already carries significant signal on all four isoforms on its own, so a charge column might be paying for something a single binary feature already has.

The atom-level arm was left pre-registered and unrun.

Detected, not material

The molecule-level question is simpler: do the quantum columns improve prediction over the free 2D descriptors they would sit alongside?

Before testing that, notebook 44 asked how much of each quantum column a cheap 2D model can already reproduce. Most of it, as it turns out.

How much of each quantum column a 226-descriptor 2D block already predicts, as an upper bound taken from the better of a linear and a nonlinear estimate. Hirshfeld charge summaries sit at 0.89 to 0.99. Only the dipole moment and two 3D shape ratios resist. Reproducibility of a feature is not the same as predictive redundancy, which is what the increment arms exist to settle.

Notebook 46 then ran the comparison properly: six feature blocks against the free-descriptor baseline on the frozen 25-fold cluster-disjoint partition, under the full Ash protocol15 with the homogeneity branch checked rather than assumed. Five of eight omnibus tests cleared, which routed to Tukey for the first time in this project, since six methods sits under the threshold above which the protocol switches to Benjamini-Hochberg.16

Every block against the free baseline on both metrics, with each isoform’s materiality bar as the dashed red line on the improving side. Six of forty cells reach significance. Not one bar reaches its line.

Six cells of forty are significant and none is material. The largest is the molecule-level block on CYP2D6 ranking, at 45% of its bar with 22 of 25 folds improving. Five of the six significant cells improve and one harms: the halogen-conditioned atom block costs CYP2C9 ranking, with only 7 of 25 folds better.

The four atom descriptors that notebook 45’s screen had recommended come in at 0 of 16 across both contrasts. Not immaterial, not significant at all. Every significant cell in the arm comes from the molecule-level block that notebook 44 had already found immaterial.

One finding did come out of it that nobody was testing for.

The electronic and shape halves of the block, tested separately against the same baseline. On CYP2C9 they are near-equal and opposite, so testing the block as one unit measured a cancellation rather than an absence. Asterisks mark raw p below 0.05; this comparison is post-hoc and is fenced as such.

Split in half, the electronic and shape columns do opposite things depending on isoform, and on CYP2C9 they very nearly cancel. The block-level null there was two real effects summing to zero, not an absence of effect. The audit of that notebook pointed out that this comparison, unlike the primaries, was formulated after the block-level null was read and sits in no pre-declared family, so the notebook now carries it fenced as post-hoc and the claim rests on CYP2C9 alone.

How a bar gets chosen

The bar is doing more work in this post than any single result, and it has now been got wrong once and disputed twice.

The rule is that a materiality bar is twice the mean standard error of a 25-fold paired comparison on this partition, pooled across ten different arms against the plain model. Pooling across arms is the point: it measures how well this design resolves any difference, independent of the one being tested. It is never twice the standard error of the comparison under test, because that is approximately the significance threshold restated and carries no information significance did not already give.

The first dispute was arithmetic. Notebook 45 found that the 25 folds live across three notebooks, and that reading them from one gives 10 folds per comparison, inflating every standard error by roughly the square root of 25 over 10.

The second showed how much the choice matters. Notebook 44 had pre-registered a ranking comparison and never run it; the audit ran it late and labelled it as such. Derived from the comparison under test, the bars come out at 0.0012 to 0.0034 and call 7 of 12 cells material. Derived the independent way, they come out 5 to 8 times larger and call none material. Both derivations and the resulting flip are printed in the notebook, because the verdict turns on the choice and a reader is entitled to see it.

The audit also found that the pre-registration file’s timestamp post-dates 459 of the 476 prediction files, and that nothing was committed to git, so there is no independent evidence of commit order. Two things limit the damage, and both are checkable: the bars reproduce exactly from a file dated five days before the experiment, which cannot encode its outcome, and refitting arms from the current feature files reproduces the stored predictions to machine epsilon, so the training data is the data that was used. What is not recoverable is the provenance of the criteria text itself, and for a pre-registered negative that is the part a reader most needs.

The same audit established that notebook 44 ran no omnibus test at all, skipping two steps the protocol specifies. Notebook 46 recorded that as a formal disclosure rather than quietly fixing it.

Two controls

With the feature route closed on accuracy, the remaining argument for the quantum block was diversity. An ensemble member does not need to be accurate if it is wrong in different places, which is the condition that makes averaging work at all.17 My current ensemble’s entire gain rests on one member, so a replacement for it would be worth having.

Notebook 49 pre-registered a gate before training: a quantum-only arm passes if its residual correlation against the pool falls below that member’s on at least one isoform. It passed, on CYP3A4, both arms.

Then I added a control that was not pre-registered, a constant predictor, and it passed the same gate on two of four isoforms, and on CYP3A4 more strongly than the real arm.

Left: the gate passed on CYP3A4, and a zero-information control passes it too, more strongly. Centre: the accuracy leg, with the QM-only arms sitting on the naive-baseline line rather than at half their bar. Right: the weight fit gives the arm exactly nothing on the isoform it passed.

The mechanism is not subtle once it is visible. Residual correlation against a pool is depressed by weakness as much as by orthogonality: a nearly constant arm’s residuals are dominated by the negative of the true values, so they correlate poorly with everyone. The quantum-only arms score 0.92 to 0.98 ST-RAE against a naive baseline of exactly 1.0, and their prediction spread runs 0.25 to 0.37 of the training-label spread against board targets of 0.82 to 0.93. They are not accurate-and-diverse. They are inaccurate, and the gate I wrote could not tell the difference.

The notebook reports that as a defect in its own design rather than as a pass. The weight fit, which cannot be fooled the same way, gives the quantum arms zero weight on CYP3A4 in all four configurations tested.

Notebook 52 then ran the one mechanism left. Aggregating 252,237 atom rows into four columns is a lossy summary; feeding per-atom values into the message passing is a different proposition, because the value attaches to the atom and travels to its neighbours. That route has real precedent for quantum features in graph networks.18

Getting there took three obstacles. CheMeleon refuses per-atom features outright in Chemprop19 2.3.1,20 established from the source, from the checkpoint shapes and from a CLI call that exits 1. The way through was a local foundation file carrying CheMeleon’s own weights widened by columns of zeros, which reproduces it exactly at initialisation. Taking that route then exposed a genuine upstream defect: on the foundation path Chemprop fits and logs the atom-feature scaler but never attaches the transform, while the dataset normalises its arrays in place, so training sees scaled features and prediction sees unscaled ones, silently, on every blind prediction. And the quantum run featurised raw SMILES while Chemprop is given canonical SMILES, so the atom orderings differ on 1,543 of 5,655 compounds and had to be mapped explicitly, with a negative control that bites on all 50 probes.

The design was three arms: the plain model, the model with quantum features, and the same model with the atom array zeroed. The zeros control is the sharper test, because dropping the flag entirely would also change the encoder and the command line.

Three arms at 25 folds. The isolation comparison, real atom values against zeros, is the blue point in each panel. Every difference sits inside the bar, and only one omnibus cleared at all.

The primary comparison is significant on 0 of 8 cells and material on 0 of 8. In the single cell whose omnibus cleared, the two arms share a compact-letter-display letter at p = 0.83.

The attribution then runs backwards for the hypothesis. The zeros control is more significant against the plain model than the real arm is, at 84% of bar against 71%. Whatever small ranking gain exists on CYP3A4 comes from the thirteen molecule-level descriptors and the model load path, not from the per-atom values. That is only visible because the control ran at the same power as the arm.

One ceiling this cannot speak past: Chemprop carries no explicit hydrogens, so 45% of the quantum atom rows never reach the graph at all. A third column was added specifically to recover the largest identified casualty of that, reproducing the per-molecule hydrogen summary exactly, and it changed nothing.

The experiment that is still waiting

One test remains built and unsent. Notebooks 50 and 51 are a matched pair: ridge on 226 free descriptors against ridge on those same 226 plus 17 quantum columns, where the feature block is the only difference. Both call one function in one script, and the second asserts its pipeline against the first’s recorded fingerprint field by field.

The part I like is what the correction chain does to the comparison. Both files get the same placement and widening procedure, which forces three of four isoforms to identical spread and CYP2D6 to an identical mean. On those three the two submissions can differ only in rank order, which is the quantity that separates the leading columns on this leaderboard and the one no affine correction can reach. Spread is designed out rather than controlled for afterwards.

Its limits are recorded too. Notebook 46 put the largest quantum effect at 24% of bar on error and 45% on ranking, and a single pair of board readings has no error bar, so the pair can detect a large difference and cannot resolve a small one. The expected macro was written down as 0.62 to 0.85 and explicitly not expected to beat the current best of 0.5982.

Neither has been sent, because the submission endpoint in both notebooks is stale: the host does not exist and the parameter set is out of date, which a later notebook found when its own gate was opened for the first time.

Where this leaves things

Three ways of asking, three failures, and the two that produced the clearest answers were decided by controls rather than by the arms.

What the quantum data did buy is real but smaller than 281 core-hours sounds. A methods result on cost, where the cheap level of theory and the expensive one sit at naive-predictor level standalone and disagree by isoform rather than uniformly. A cancellation finding, where testing a block as one unit measured two opposing effects summing to zero. A chemistry bind stated precisely enough to be useful to someone else: the definition faithful to the coordination chemistry cannot work as a feature, and the one that works is narrower than the chemistry supports.

And a rule I now trust more than I did, which is that a bar has to come from the design’s own noise rather than from the comparison being tested. Getting that wrong once, and watching the verdict flip on 7 of 12 cells depending on which derivation I used, was worth more than the descriptors were.

None of this says the quantum data is uninformative in principle. It says that on 4,905 compounds, against a 226-column 2D block, through three different mechanisms, it does not convert into accuracy or ranking that clears the resolution of the design measuring it. Independent re-evaluations of published ADMET models report plenty of effects that do not survive contact with a held-out set,21 and this is one more, caught before it was submitted rather than after.

entry.title: To split or not to split

link.title: To split or not to split

entry.content:
What this post covers

By the end of the last post I had four occasions where a cross-validated result failed to reach the leaderboard,1 each with stronger CV backing than the last. The common factor I kept coming back to was the split: every one of those decisions had been made on a random partition, and three entrants above me use cluster-disjoint folds.

This post covers building that partition properly, what happened to the result that motivated it, and the two submissions that came out of the work. Every score below is a half-set measurement.

A split that should have mattered

Pat Walters confirmed on the challenge Discord that CYP3A4’s screening set was itself built by Butina clustering,2 at 2048-bit Morgan radius 33 with a Tanimoto distance cutoff of 0.65, pairing each qualifying hit with a random cluster-mate. How a dataset is split materially affects what an evaluation measures,4 and a design that does not resemble how the test set was built can estimate prospective performance badly.5 If the test set was constructed by clustering, a random training split is measuring something the blind set does not ask for.

Notebook 33 built a single cluster-disjoint partition on that recipe. It produced 2,617 clusters over the 4,905 curated compounds, and 78.8% of compounds changed fold membership relative to the frozen random partition, against the roughly 80% two independent partitions would give.

Held-out compounds under the cluster-disjoint scheme sit at a median nearest-neighbour similarity of 0.365 to their own fold’s training portion, against 0.438 under the random scheme. The blind set sits at 0.587. So the new partition moves held-out compounds away from the blind set’s profile, not towards it. The case for using this split is not that it looks more like the real test set.

The AID 1851 auxiliary-head arm against the plain model on both partitions. On the random partition the arm came out ahead on three isoforms of four by sign, significantly so only on CYP2D6. On the Butina partition every isoform changed sign. The real leaderboard agreed with Butina and disagreed with random CV, which looked like evidence that my split decision had been misleading model selection for months.

It was five folds, one partition, one seed per fold.

Two reasons that answer was wrong

Notebook 34 was supposed to be the confirmation. It found two problems with notebook 33 before it got anywhere near a result.

The first is that the partition itself was not reproducible. Notebook 33 broke ties by lowest fold index; the repeated design breaks them by the repeat’s seed. Recomputing the clustering gives the same 2,617 clusters size for size, but the fold assignment does not match: best-case agreement between notebook 33’s folds and repeat 0 is 22.4%. Notebook 33’s numbers therefore sit on a partition no later notebook ever used.

The second, before training notebook 34 retrains the plain model on the random partition’s fold zero and compares against notebook 05’s stored score, with a hard stop above 0.03. It came back at 0.0378 and aborted, before any of the 125 planned training units started.

The input CSV was byte-identical to notebook 05’s. The chemprop6 command line was identical to notebook 31’s. The validation loss was bit-identical for epochs 0 and 1, then diverged at epoch 2. The data and the initialisation were right and the arithmetic was not. The cause was OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, inherited from notebook 33’s setup cell, which changes the order of floating-point reductions and so the training trajectory. Unset, it reproduced notebook 05 exactly, 0.00000000 on all four isoforms.

Notebook 33 ran under that setting, and it never ran this check, correctly noting that no stored external comparison exists for a brand-new partition. Its own arm-versus-arm comparisons are internally consistent, since both arms ran the same way. Its absolute Butina numbers are not on the same numerical footing as the random-partition numbers, which is the comparison it drew.

What twenty-five folds said

I ran the design out properly, in three stages: two repeats in notebook 34 (10 folds, 100 training units, 11.42 h), a third in notebook 35 (15 folds), and the last two in notebook 37, reaching the 5 × 5 design Ash et al. specify as the minimum for this kind of comparison.7 Eleven arms, 275 units in total.

Every analysis reports the lower fold count beside the higher one, which is the check that adding folds was not a selection. The largest shift in any arm’s mean ST-RAE between 15 and 25 folds is 0.0132.

The flip count:

Design Sign-resolved cells Flips
Notebook 33, 5 folds 4 4
Notebook 34, 10 folds 25 1
Notebook 35, 15 folds 25 0
Notebook 37, 25 folds 25 0

The first row is not on the same footing as the rest: notebook 33 compared one arm across four isoforms and applied no resolution rule, where the later rows cover all eleven arms under one. A cell counts as a flip only where both partitions resolve a sign, meaning the absolute mean difference exceeds its own standard error, which is itself a noisier quantity than it looks.8 That rule exists because notebook 34’s first apparent flip turned out to be a +0.000019 near-tie in notebook 05’s own numbers.

The one flip at ten folds was the AID arm on CYP3A4. At fifteen folds that cell no longer resolves a sign at all.

Every arm measured twice, once on each partition, with the pair joined so it reads as one object. A pair straddling the zero line would be a sign flip. There are none: 0 of 6 on CYP1A2, 0 of 7 on CYP2C9, 0 of 5 on CYP2D6 and 0 of 7 on CYP3A4, with 11 cells unresolved and the single-task arm carrying no random-partition reference at all.

Ordering agreement between the two partitions runs 0.99, 0.96, 0.84 and 0.99 by isoform, and the best arm on both partitions is the same arm on all four.

So the split design does not explain the four board failures. The hypothesis was testable and it failed, and the version of it I had believed for a fortnight rested on a partition I could not reproduce and a threading setting that moved the third decimal place.

The arm that did work

The same runs turned up something I was not looking for.

The dead-zone target, from two posts ago, replaces the training target with clip(oof_prediction, conf_low, conf_high) under absolute-error loss, so a compound the model already places inside its own published credible band contributes no gradient. At 25 cluster-disjoint folds it is significantly better than the plain model on all four isoforms, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected,9 improving on every one of the 25 folds on CYP1A2, CYP2C9 and CYP2D6, and on 23 of 25 for CYP3A4.

Compact letter display, eleven arms by four isoforms. The dead-zone arm holds tier a on all four, and the “tied with best” colour appears nowhere: no other arm shares the top letter on any isoform.

It is the only arm that does that. The macro ordering puts it at 0.6723, against 0.7331 for the loss-function-only variant, 0.7517 for the AID arm and 0.7654 for the plain model.

The decomposition matters, because the dead-zone arm changes two things at once: the loss function and the target. A loss-only arm isolates the first. At 25 folds the clipping carries 64% of the gain on CYP1A2, 86% on CYP2C9, 34% on CYP2D6 and 95% on CYP3A4. On three of four isoforms the clipping is doing most of the work, and CYP2D6 is the exception in the other direction. That pattern holds at 10, 15 and 25 folds, and it held on the random partition’s single-fold screen as well, so it looks like a property of the isoform rather than of the design.

The AID arm, by contrast, resolves against the plain model on one isoform of four at the completed design. It also resolved on one at ten folds, but not the same one: CYP2D6 then, CYP1A2 now.

One other thing came out of the run. The tree models on raw fingerprint and descriptor features are the first genuinely decorrelated arms this project has produced, measured on residuals rather than on raw predictions.10 Mordred11 descriptors reduced by PCA, with XGBoost,12 sit below the error-correlation floor on all four isoforms, where the dead-zone, loss-only and single-task arms all sit above it. They are also substantially worse on their own. Whether that trade is worth anything is the question the rest of this post is about.

Closing the correction route

Running in parallel with all of this was the correction work, which is where every board gain to date had come from.

Notebook 36 applied a spread widening to notebook 32’s submitted columns, with each isoform’s target taken from the spread ratio of whichever submitted column holds that isoform’s best score, and a 10% relative-gap bar below which nothing is touched. Three isoforms were widened and CYP2D6 was left alone, its column already sitting on target from an earlier correction. It scored macro 0.6270, and all three widened isoforms improved, which was the prediction recorded before sending.

The interesting part is that two of them were treated almost identically and behaved completely differently. CYP2C9 took a 1.1304 multiplier from an 11.5% gap and gained 0.0200. CYP3A4 took 1.1317 from an 11.6% gap and gained 0.0003.

Notebook 38 went after that. Writing R² = 2ρk − k² − b², with k the ratio of prediction spread to population spread and b the standardised bias, following the decomposition another entrant on this challenge set out in their own working notes,13 the blind CYP3A4 population can be fitted by least squares across all eleven submissions on record. Two changes from the earlier solve: Pearson ρ is recovered from the published Spearman through ρ = 2 sin(πρS/6) rather than substituted raw, which was algebraically infeasible on 5 of 11 rows, and no MAE term is used, so there is no residual-normality assumption and no sign ambiguity.

The fit gives a blind CYP3A4 mean of 4.778 and a standard deviation of 1.397, with an RMS residual of 0.0065 on R². It then passed a real out-of-sample test: fitted before notebook 36’s submission was scored, it predicted that column’s CYP3A4 R² at 0.6515 against a measured 0.6563.

Applied to the 0.0613 gap between my CYP3A4 column and the best on record, the decomposition is 117% correlation and −17% placement, with scale zero by construction. The widened column is better centred than the one beating it. A perfect placement correction would recover 0.0051 of R².

That closes the route. Every board improvement this project had made up to that point came from affine corrections, and affine corrections cannot change rank order. On the isoform where I am strongest, rank order is all that is left.

One object, not four

Which pushed the remaining work towards ensembling, and towards a claim I had been carrying as settled since notebook 35.

That claim was that CYP2D6 cannot be blended. Greedy selection with replacement14 collapsed to a single member on that isoform, at 25 of 25 folds in the completed design, and I had recorded it as a stable property rather than an artefact.

Notebook 39 showed it was an artefact of what the per-isoform search optimises. Comparing three levels of constraint, with the member set and the weights refitted inside each fold and scored on the held-out one:

Constraint Nested macro ST-RAE
No blend 0.7600
Per-isoform members and weights 0.6529
One shared member set, per-isoform weights 0.6531
One shared member set and one shared weight vector 0.6502

The most constrained version generalises best, and it wins almost entirely on CYP2D6, which improves by 0.0113 while carrying two members its own per-isoform search rejects at all 25 folds. Read as regularisation, the per-isoform search was overfitting its own folds.

That result also happens to serve a preference I had already stated for its own reasons: I would rather submit one model or one ensemble output than a per-isoform assembly of different models, which is what my best submission is.

What the board said

Two submissions came out of this stretch.

The first, notebook 47, is the loss-function-only model retrained on all 4,905 compounds. It is the leak-free half of the dead-zone effect, since its targets are the literal curated labels and it carries none of the fold-crosstalk exposure the dead-zone target has. It scored macro 0.6328, and its CYP2C9 column came in at 0.5255, a new best on record, beating the 0.5375 held jointly by four earlier submissions.

The second, notebook 48, is a per-isoform non-negative ensemble fitted on the completed 25-fold design and deployed on full-data blind columns. Before sending it, I measured the blend against its own best single component on resolution bars frozen two days earlier, derived from how well a 25-fold paired comparison on this partition resolves any difference rather than the one under test.

The ensemble against its best single component on both metrics, with the frozen bars marked. Two isoforms clear; two do not.

CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 cleared on both metrics, at 121% and 125% of the ST-RAE bar and 156% and 183% of the Spearman bar. CYP2C9 and CYP2D6 were significant and under their bars, which on this project’s own adoption rule is not an established case.

It scored 0.6356. CYP1A2’s Spearman fell 0.0316 and CYP3A4’s moved 0.0011. Both isoforms the analysis had resolved as material regressed. CYP2C9, the isoform it had explicitly set aside as unresolvable and left uncorrected, set the highest Spearman on record at 0.7692.

The fitted weights, and the member the whole gain rests on. Removing the AID arm collapses the greedy blend onto a single member on all four isoforms.

The reason was written down before the submission went out. The entire measured gain rests on the AID arm: drop that member and the greedy fit collapses onto the dead-zone model alone on all four isoforms, with a gain of exactly zero. The AID arm is also the one member where out-of-fold and board evidence can be compared without a correction in the way, and they disagree, with the board preferring the plain model on all four isoforms by 0.043 to 0.149 ST-RAE. The prediction file carried that counterexample in writing, and it is what bit.

Neither submission beat 27b, which has held at 0.5982 since 19 September.

Where this leaves things

The month’s largest piece of work tested a hypothesis about my own methodology and the hypothesis failed. Zero of twenty-five sign-resolved comparisons flip between the two partitions, the arm ordering agrees at 0.84 to 0.99, and the same arm wins on both. Cluster-disjoint splitting does not change this project’s conclusions.

What the apparatus produced instead is a defensible comparison under the protocol the literature specifies, one arm that beats the baseline everywhere under it, and a placement solve that passed an out-of-sample test and then told me the remaining gap on my strongest isoform is ranking, which no correction I have can reach.

The ensemble result is the one I keep going back to. It is the first transfer failure here where the cross-validated effect was material on both metrics rather than merely significant, measured against a bar frozen before the comparison existed, and on the two isoforms it resolved, one regressed and the other did not move. Independent re-evaluations of published ADMET models report the same pattern at field scale.15 Four CV-to-board failures have become five, and this one was the most carefully gated of them.

entry.title: Model report: the interim submission
entry.content:
A reference post for the intermediate leaderboard checkpoint on 24 September.1 Eleven submissions condensed into what the model is, what the record shows and what the reveal will test.

Two different kinds of change have been made over those eleven submissions and they aren’t judged on the same metric.

Model changes alter which compounds the model thinks are more potent. They show up in board Spearman and Kendall. Nothing else moves these numbers.

Post-hoc corrections alter where a whole prediction column sits on the axis and how wide it is. They are affine, so they cannot reorder anything. They show up in ST-RAE, MAE and R², and leave Spearman and Kendall fixed by construction.

Conflating the two is the easiest way to misread this leaderboard. CYP2D6’s R² went from −0.59 to +0.41 across three submissions without a single prediction changing rank, which is this project’s clearest demonstration that a poor leaderboard score can be explained by a badly placed model.

Every figure below is a half-set measurement: the live board scores half the blind test set, split by chemical series and the full set is scored only at the reveal and at the close on 3 November.

The result

Best submission to date, 27b, submitted 2026-09-19:

  Macro CYP1A2 CYP2C9 CYP2D6 CYP3A4
ST-RAE 0.5982 0.6954 0.5375 0.7165 0.4434
MAE 0.7206 0.9385 0.5280 0.8975 0.5183
R² 0.4835 0.3073 0.5432 0.4124 0.6709
Spearman 0.7002 0.7375 0.7585 0.4872 0.8177

Lower ST-RAE is better; a constant predictor scores exactly 1.0 by construction. Best macro ST-RAE, R², Spearman and Kendall of any submission this project has made, from 0.7179 on the first.

Macro ST-RAE across the first seven submissions. Filled circles changed the model; open diamonds changed only a post-hoc correction. Every improvement is a diamond. The four submissions since follow the same shape: two model changes that lost on ST-RAE, one correction that produced the result above.

What the submission actually is

Not one model. Each isoform’s column comes from whichever recipe holds that isoform’s best real board result.

Isoform Column Correction
CYP1A2 Single CheMeleon-initialised multitask Chemprop, full-data retrain none
CYP2C9 Capped Caruana-weighted ensemble none
CYP2D6 The same Chemprop architecture plus four AID 1851 auxiliary heads placement, then spread
CYP3A4 Single CheMeleon-initialised multitask Chemprop, full-data retrain none

The base model throughout is a directed message-passing neural network2,3 initialised from the CheMeleon foundation checkpoint,4 trained multitask across all four isoforms under a masked loss, since 73% of compounds carry a label for exactly one enzyme.

Three columns are raw model outputs whilst CYP2D6 carries an offset landing it on a blind population mean solved from the board’s own published metrics, then a spread scale widening it to 0.85 of the training-label standard deviation.

Model changes: what improved ranking

Board Spearman per isoform, across every model this project has submitted. Only a model change can move these numbers, so this is the honest record of whether any modelling work paid off.

Isoform Plain model Caruana ensemble + AID 1851 + AID and dead-zone Best
CYP1A2 0.7375 0.7389 0.7466 0.7565 dead-zone + AID
CYP2C9 0.7389 0.7585 0.7333 0.7554 Caruana ensemble
CYP2D6 0.4000 0.3771 0.4872 0.4438 AID 1851
CYP3A4 0.8177 0.7706 0.7651 0.8020 plain model

External data is the only change that improved blind ranking on the most difficult isoform. CYP2D6’s rank correlation sat at 0.40 across five submissions, two ensembling methods and three calibration mechanisms. Adding 16,459 compounds from PubChem AID 1851, an NCATS quantitative high-throughput cytochrome panel covering 17,143 compounds against five isozymes,5,6 as auxiliary prediction heads moved it to 0.4872 and that gain is in the current submission. Every internal lever tried before left it ranking flat or worse.

The submission is not on the best-ranked column for CYP1A2. The dead-zone model ranks CYP1A2 better than the plain model, 0.7565 against 0.7375, and scored worse on ST-RAE, 0.7906 against 0.6954. That is a placement problem and likely has some unexploited headroom.

Corrections: what improved placement

One metric throughout, CYP2D6’s board ST-RAE, with Spearman alongside to show that no correction touched the ranking.

Change CYP2D6 ST-RAE Spearman
Uncorrected plain model 1.1673 0.4000
Recentred on the solved blind population 0.8299 0.4000
Spread widened to 0.85 of training SD 0.7858 0.4000
Same two corrections on the AID model 0.7165 0.4872

Spearman moves exactly once, on the row where the model changed. The improvement from 1.1673 to 0.7858 was produced entirely by arithmetic on predictions already made.

CYP2D6’s R² (top) and Spearman (bottom) across the first seven submissions. R² crosses zero when recentring is applied; Spearman barely moves. The Spearman axis is fixed to 0 to 1 rather than autoscaled, so its flatness is shown honestly.

The ordering was always roughly right and the whole column sat in the wrong place on the axis.

The raw prediction column (grey) and the recentred one (red), with the solved blind population as a dashed Normal curve. The correction moves the column 1.35 log units.

The second lever is spread. Models trained on this data compress toward the mean, under-prediction costs 1.65 to 2.79 times more than over-prediction under this metric and compression is measurable against the real board rather than only out of fold. Another entrant, running under the name 450 nm, publishes a per-isoform table on their own operating dashboard showing their board ST-RAE rank ordered by exactly that.7

Prediction spread relative to training-label spread against board ST-RAE. Coloured points are this project’s submissions; crosses are an external entrant’s. Pooled Spearman −0.822.

What the correction method actually is

It is leaderboard probing and should be called that.

The method is not mine. It comes from SuperCowPowers’ working notes on this challenge, which decompose R² into a correlation term, a spread-ratio term and a bias term, and use an affine fit to recalibrate where predictions sit.8 I first applied the decomposition against this project’s own training population, where the scale and bias terms accounted for almost nothing. Applied against the blind population, the same algebra gives the population directly: a submission’s own prediction mean and standard deviation are known exactly, so with its published R² and MAE the blind mean and spread follow as two equations in two unknowns. The CYP2D6 corrections in this submission are that approach applied to this project’s own board results, nothing more.

That information comes from the test labels. It reaches me through the published metrics rather than through the labels themselves, but that is a difference of route, not of kind. None of it generalises to a setting where no leaderboard is answering.

Three risks follow, in order of how much they worry me.

The board scores half the blind set, split by chemical series. Every solved moment and the 0.85 spread scale are fitted to that half. If the halves differ in composition and a split by chemical series is designed to make them differ, the corrections are tuned to a population that is not the one scored at the reveal. The 1.35 log unit CYP2D6 offset is the most exposed single number in the submission.

Per-isoform selection across eleven board readings carries no multiple-comparison correction. The current recipe picks, for each isoform, whichever of eleven submissions scored best on that isoform. Every cross-validation comparison in this project is Benjamini-Hochberg corrected.9 On the board side there is no correction at all and that selection is the whole recipe.

The sign of the offset is not recoverable from the algebra. R² and MAE depend on the bias only through its magnitude, so every solution has a mirror image producing identical metrics. CYP2D6’s resolution rests on a convention adopted from an external precedent8 plus a convergence check not a derivation.

What did not work

Board rows are blind evidence; CV rows are not, and are marked as such.

Approach Tested on Result Why
Ensembling: simple averages, capped Caruana10 Board, twice Macro 0.8299 both times, against 0.7138 Error correlations of 0.79 to 0.91: the members get the same compounds wrong. Kept for CYP2C9 only, where it gave the best rank on record (0.7585)
Calibration toward AID 1851 population moments Board Macro 0.8811 Worse on every isoform. Only calibration toward the blind population has helped
Dead-zone target on the AID model Board Macro 0.6488 CYP2D6 worse on both ranking and placement like for like (ST-RAE 0.7502 vs 0.7165, Spearman 0.4438 vs 0.4872). Raw columns all worse than the plain model’s. Improved CYP1A2 ranking only
Non-negative stacking CV only Beat best single config out of fold Never submitted. The coefficient cancellation diagnosed elsewhere11 is absent from this pool
Butina and analog-holdout splits CV Inconclusive; analog holdout widened the CV-to-blind gap 2.3 to 9.3× A split mimicking blind-set construction made the gap larger, not smaller
Net charge at pH 7.412 as a descriptor CV Tied on all four isoforms Real correlation with pIC50, but error correlation against baseline 0.984 to 0.990
Inverse-density sample weighting CV Significantly worse, both configs Starved the dense middle where most compounds sit
Interval-aware training objective CV 0.06 to 0.12 log unit gap Real, too small to justify a custom loss
Retrieved near-neighbour corpus Not built Closed off Hard compounds are not structurally distant from training on any isoform

The claim that four cross-validated results failed to transfer compares raw board ST-RAE, which confounds ranking with placement. On ranking, the AID result did transfer, on the isoform it was predicted to help; what failed was its ST-RAE, because the better-ranked model was also more compressed. Two of the four failed on both ranking and placement. The broader pattern is not peculiar to this project: independent re-evaluations of published ADMET models on held-out data report the same at field scale.13

A pre-registered prediction for the reveal

Recorded before the full set is scored, so the gap can be read as a measure of board overfit rather than explained after the fact.

The three uncorrected columns should transfer roughly intact. CYP2D6’s corrections are the exposed part. If they carry to the unseen half, the full-set macro lands near the half-set 0.5982. If they fail completely and CYP2D6 reverts on the unseen half toward its uncorrected 1.3168, its full-set value lands near 1.02 and macro near 0.673.

Point prediction: macro ST-RAE 0.64, with 0.60 to 0.68 covering the plausible range.

The diagnostic is CYP2D6 specifically, not the macro. If its full-set ST-RAE comes back above about 1.0, the population solve did not generalise across the series split, and every corrected submission on this project is worth less than its half-set score suggested. If it comes back near 0.72, the solve found a real population property rather than a property of half of one.

Summary

Ranking improved once, on CYP2D6, and only when compounds from outside the challenge entered the training pool. Every internal rearrangement left it flat or worse.

Placement improved three times, all by arithmetic on predictions already made, worth 0.45 ST-RAE on CYP2D6 alone and most of the project’s macro improvement.

The reveal tests placement much harder than ranking. Ranking is a property of the model and should survive a change of scoring population. Placement, here, is a property of half a leaderboard.

entry.title: Four confirmations, four board failures
entry.content:
What this post covers

Two modelling ideas, both tested more carefully than anything else in this project, both confirmed on cross-validation, and both worse than the baseline when they reached the real leaderboard. Then the part that matters: one of those two failures turned out to be a calibration artefact rather than a verdict on the model, and correcting for that produced the best submission this project has made.

Four submissions, macro ST-RAE, every figure a half-set measurement:1

Submission What it was Macro
NB27-widened CYP2D6 spread widened, from the last post 0.6155
NB30 AID 1851 auxiliary heads, raw, no correction 0.8160
27b The same model, CYP2D6 corrected 0.5982
NB32-A Dead-zone target on top of that model 0.6488

Training on compounds from outside the challenge

Every entrant materially above me trains on more compounds than my 4,905. The auxiliary-head mechanism from two posts ago pays where it brings new compounds into the shared encoder’s pool and costs where it only adds columns, which is the multitask picture reported elsewhere for ADME endpoints: extra tasks help most where they supply data a sparse endpoint does not have.2,3 The challenge’s own released files are exhausted on that front. PubChem AID 1851, an NCATS quantitative high-throughput cytochrome panel covering 17,143 compounds against five isozymes,4,5 was already fetched and curated back when I used it as a calibration target and it failed badly in that role. That failure says nothing about this one. Calibration asks an external population for a centre; auxiliary heads ask it for gradient signal.

The gate came first: does AID 1851 track my own measured pIC50 on the compounds where both exist? This matters more than it might sound, because potency values aggregated across different assays and laboratories carry substantial systematic noise,6 and AID 1851 is a bioluminescent assay while the challenge’s own data is fluorescence and mass spectrometry. Frozen criteria on disk before a single correlation was computed. Two things came out of it that I did not expect.

The first is that my own sparse labelling, not the external assay, is the binding constraint. Only 98 compounds overlap, and per isoform only 20 to 49 of those carry a non-null label, because each isoform column is 26 to 48% populated. The criterion as originally drafted required at least 200 overlapping compounds, which is arithmetically unsatisfiable here. I amended it to n of at least 20 plus a bootstrap confidence requirement, before computing anything, because freezing an unsatisfiable criterion would have produced a guaranteed fail on sample size rather than evidence about the assay.

The second is that the curated file I had been carrying since notebook 13 is worse than it looks. Its potency column exists for every row, but 49.7% of those values are censoring floors rather than measurements: where no dose-response curve fitted, the value is the top tested concentration. Every efficacy readout was silently dropped at the aggregation step, and those columns are recorded at 100% coverage whether or not a curve fitted. They were still sitting in the raw batch files.

That distinction decides the whole exercise. The argument for AID 1851 as training signal is that it supplies the compounds that did nothing, which my training set lacks by construction because the organisers promoted only top hits to dose-response. Under the potency readout, most of those 16,459 new compounds arrive carrying one of five repeated floor constants. Under efficacy they arrive carrying a real graded number.

The potency readout has the higher headline correlation (0.79 on CYP1A2 against efficacy’s 0.54), and it is the one that cleared the frozen gate. It also does not survive a sensitivity check on half the isoforms: strip the floored values out and CYP2C9’s correlation flips sign from +0.35 to −0.25, and CYP3A4’s rests on eight real fits. Efficacy is weaker at its peak but uniform, 0.48 to 0.64 on all four isoforms, every value a measurement. I went with efficacy, and recorded the prior pointing the other way: the Emax arm two posts ago was also an efficacy-type readout and it hurt CYP1A2.

Single-fold screen, three seeds, held-out ST-RAE. All four isoforms move the right way; two resolve against the frozen rule.

All four isoforms improved, two of them resolving as genuine improvements against the frozen threshold, with CYP1A2’s three AID seeds sitting entirely below its three baseline seeds. Every secondary metric moved the same way on every isoform. After eight screens that came back flat or below seed noise, this was the first resolved improvement the project had produced.

It was also one fold.

Confirming it properly

Twenty-five folds, two arms, one seed per fold taken from the frozen manifest so the numbers stay comparable with the original CV comparison. Fifty real training runs of a CheMeleon-initialised directed message-passing network,7,8 about seventeen hours of compute. Paired tests, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected,9 with the homogeneity-of-variance branch checked rather than assumed, following the comparison protocol this project has used throughout.10

One deliberate change from the screen, and it is a correction rather than a variation. The screen computed its winsorisation bounds once, on one fold’s training portion. Carrying those fixed values across 25 folds would clip 24 of them using bounds computed partly from their own held-out compounds. Small, but a leak, and the kind that is easy to miss because nothing about it looks like a train-test overlap.11 Recomputed per fold, the bounds barely move, which makes the size of the avoided leak visible instead of assumed.

Each line is one fold, baseline to AID arm. Black is the mean. CYP1A2 and CYP2D6 carry the effect; CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 do not.

The screen’s headline did not survive. CYP1A2 is significantly better (−0.0462, 95% CI −0.0713 to −0.0212, p 0.0017 after correction, 20 of 25 folds improving). CYP2D6 is significantly better and larger still (−0.0670, dz −1.01, p 0.00014, 21 of 25 folds). CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 are indistinguishable from zero, p 0.507 and 0.179, CIs spanning zero. Two of four verdicts reproduced.

CYP2D6 is the biggest number in the table and the least usable one, for the reason it has always been: out-of-fold ST-RAE is not a valid selection metric for that isoform, and the board has contradicted out-of-fold evidence for it twice. Banking the largest effect in the run because it is the largest is exactly what that caveat exists to prevent.

This is still the strongest modelling evidence this project has produced. A properly powered, paired, corrected repeated-measures result on the project’s own frozen partition, on the first lever tested here that adds information rather than rearranging it.

Submitting it raw

The full-data retrain went out uncorrected, deliberately. Every board gain so far has come from post-hoc correction of the same underlying model’s predictions, and both of those corrections were fitted to that specific model’s prediction distribution. A different model produces a different distribution and neither transfers. Submitting raw is also what makes an honest re-derivation possible later, since the population solve needs an uncorrected column and its own published metrics to work from.13

Before sending it, I wrote down what should happen and saved it to disk. It should score worse than the current best, which carries a CYP2D6 correction this one does not. The comparison that actually tests the model is against the last uncorrected submission of the plain model, macro 0.7138. CYP1A2 and CYP2D6 should improve against it, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 should be roughly unchanged. And a confirmed CV gain is not a guaranteed board gain.

One thing the notebook flagged that was not in the plan at all:

The AID model’s raw blind predictions (red) against the plain model’s (grey) and the training labels (shaded). Spread ratios annotated. This model is more compressed on every isoform.

Spread ratios of 0.685, 0.726, 0.415 and 0.798, against the plain model’s 0.836, 0.817, 0.608 and 0.933. More compressed on all four. Given the pooled association from the last post, and the per-isoform table another entrant publishes on their own operating dashboard showing the same ordering on their submissions,12 that is a warning sign, and it was recorded before submission rather than after.

The board came back at macro 0.8160. Worse than the plain uncorrected baseline on all four isoforms. It is the largest single-step regression in this project’s history, and it followed the most rigorous confirmation the project has ever run.

The compression signal, available before submission, pointed the right way. The significance tests carried no information about it at all.

The part that changes the reading

A raw board score conflates two things. Placement and spread are affine corrections, and affine corrections cannot change rank order, so Spearman is the one published metric that reports on the model itself rather than on where its predictions happen to sit.

Isoform Plain model AID model Direction
CYP1A2 0.7375 0.7466 slightly better
CYP2C9 0.7389 0.7333 slightly worse
CYP2D6 0.4000 0.4872 markedly better
CYP3A4 0.8177 0.7651 materially worse

CYP2D6 is a better-ranked model sitting in a badly placed, badly compressed column. That is the exact failure mode this project has already corrected twice. CYP3A4’s ranking is genuinely worse, and no correction reaches a worse ranking, so CYP3A4 has no case under this model in any form.

That decomposition is what justifies a mixed recipe rather than adopting or discarding the AID model wholesale. CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 stay on the plain model, CYP2C9 keeps its best column, and CYP2D6 takes the AID model’s column with both corrections applied.

Solving for the blind CYP2D6 population from this submission’s own published metrics gave a useful check as a side effect. The original solve used four submissions of an entirely different model, two weeks earlier. This one used a single submission of a different architecture. They agree to 0.18% on the mean and 0.05% on the spread, and both sit close to the figure SuperCowPowers report independently for the same population.13 Two solves under the same two approximations is not an independent method, but that convergence is not something a fitted artefact of one model’s errors would produce.

The corrected candidate went out and scored macro ST-RAE 0.5982, the best submission this project has made. CYP2D6’s own column came in at 0.7165, better than the plain model’s best corrected result of 0.7858.

Three predictions held. CYP2D6’s Spearman and Kendall reproduced the AID model’s own raw values exactly, 0.4872 and 0.3415, because the correction chain is affine. The three carried-over columns reproduced on every metric. That is the third separate confirmation that identical inputs produce identical board output, and the third time the rank-preservation prediction has held.

The general lesson is worth stating plainly, because it took a 0.8160 to learn it. On this challenge, a raw uncorrected submission is not a fair test of a model. The raw reading said the AID architecture was a regression. The corrected reading of the same architecture says the opposite for the one isoform that differs between them.

A training target that can reorder

Everything above is either a new model or an affine correction. There is a third category, and it is the only thing in this project that has moved rank order on purpose.

The scoring metric is zero anywhere inside a compound’s published credible band. Every model I have trained optimises squared error against the point estimate, which spends gradient chasing noise inside a band where the metric is already indifferent. So: replace the training target with clip(oof_prediction, conf_low, conf_high) under absolute-error loss. A compound the model already places inside its own band contributes nothing; a compound outside it contributes fully. Because bands have different widths, this moves compounds by different amounts, which means it can reorder them.

The target has to come from genuinely out-of-fold predictions or the whole thing collapses into a model fitting its own overfitted output. The guard that catches that is the hit rate: an in-fold model would put nearly every training row inside its own band. Measured hit rates were 18 to 42%, nowhere near it.

Four arms per isoform: baseline, the loss-function-only diagnostic, the dead-zone target, and dead-zone plus AID heads. ST-RAE on top, Spearman below with equal prominence.

The first unanimous clean win in this project’s screening history. ST-RAE improves on all four isoforms, each by 4.5 to 6 times its own baseline seed spread, and Spearman rises on all four too. Spearman is the finding that matters, because it is the one thing no affine correction in this project could ever have moved.

Two confounds got flagged in review before that result could be treated as submission-ready, and both are real.

The dead-zone arm changes two things at once, the loss function and the target. I added a diagnostic arm afterwards that changes only the loss, which is not blind to the result and is labelled as such. On every isoform, the loss change alone recovers a substantial share of the gain. The clipping mechanism still contributes its own effect on top, on three of four isoforms, with CYP2D6’s gain mostly attributable to the loss function alone.

The second confound is fold crosstalk: every dead-zone target came from a donor model that had itself been trained on this screen’s own held-out fold. That is structural, not a bug, and it plausibly inflates the screen’s measured magnitude. It does not apply to a blind submission, since no donor model has ever seen a blind compound, and it does not affect the direction of the result.

Not confirming it, and why

I combined the dead-zone target with the AID architecture and retrained on full data without running a fresh 25-fold confirmation of that specific combination. That is a deliberate deviation from this project’s own standard and I want the reasoning on the record rather than buried.

The AID arm’s own confirmation cost about seventeen hours. Confirming the combination would cost roughly the same again. Against that: the combination rests on one confirmed mechanism and one screened mechanism, the screen’s own magnitude carries the crosstalk caveat above, and by that point two CV-confirmed results had already reversed on the board, one of them the most rigorous confirmation the project had run. A 25-fold confirmation had a poor record of predicting transfer here specifically.

That is a reason to weigh the cost of a further confirmation against its track record, not a reason to abandon rigour generally. It is still the weakest-evidenced submission this project has sent.

CYP2D6 raw, after placement, and after widening, against the solved blind population. Same recipe as the two corrections before it, using this model’s own out-of-fold rho.

Two candidates got built. One takes all four columns from the new model, which risks the macro on an unconfirmed claim but is the only way to learn whether the screen’s all-four improvement transfers. The other keeps three board-validated columns and changes only CYP2D6. I sent the first, because the second learns nothing about the question the screen actually raised.

It scored macro 0.6488, worse than the corrected AID submission, and worse than the appropriate per-isoform reference on all four isoforms.

The unsent candidate’s score is computable rather than guessable, because it shares the submitted one’s CYP2D6 column byte for byte. It works out at 0.6066, also worse. The submission slot was correctly not spent on it.

Spearman again separates what happened. CYP1A2’s ranking genuinely improved, 0.7375 to 0.7565, while its ST-RAE got worse, which makes it a placement or spread problem rather than a model regression on that isoform. CYP2D6’s ranking genuinely declined against the plain AID model, 0.4872 to 0.4438, and no correction reaches that.

That is four occasions now where a cross-validated result has failed to transfer to the board. Ensembles selected on a single CV pass, which is the selection-bias failure mode the ensemble selection literature warns about directly.14 A single-fold screen whose verdict did not survive re-confirmation. A full paired corrected 5×5 confirmation. And a single-fold screen combined with an already-confirmed architecture. Each carried stronger CV backing than the last. None transferred cleanly. Independent re-evaluations of published ADMET models on held-out data report the same pattern at field scale,15 and it is the reason blind challenges exist at all.16

The record gap

One process failure is worth recording because it caught me twice in three days, in the same shape.

Both of the last four submissions were sent by hand, outside any notebook session. The canonical record of every submission is a document in the repository, and it lagged reality both times. Two separate notebooks then read that document, found no entry for a submission that had really happened, and concluded their own briefs were wrong about what the current best was. Both notebooks had a standing rule to verify every quoted figure against its source before use, and that rule is the reason this project has caught several genuinely wrong numbers. Here it fired correctly and drew the wrong conclusion, because the source of truth was stale rather than the claim.

Neither correction is retracted in either notebook. They stand as a record of what was believed when those notebooks ran, with a post-hoc note appended. The fix is not a better verification rule, it is closing the gap between a submission happening and the record reflecting it.

Where this leaves things

Macro ST-RAE has gone from 0.7179 to 0.5982 across eleven submissions. Almost all of that came from correcting where predictions sit rather than from changing how they are produced. Two of the most carefully evidenced modelling changes in the project both lost on the board, one of them spectacularly, and the one that recovered did so through correction rather than through the model.

What has genuinely changed is what a board score means to me. A raw score confounds model quality with placement, and Spearman is the only published metric that separates them. Read that way, the AID architecture is better-ranked on CYP2D6 and worse on CYP3A4, and the dead-zone model is better-ranked on CYP1A2 and worse on CYP2D6. None of that was visible in the ST-RAE column that made both look like failures.

The intermediate reveal is on the 24th, and it scores the full blind set rather than the half every figure above is measured on. Every ranking in this post is provisional against that.

entry.summary: External training data, a dead-zone training target, two full-data retrains that lost on the board, and the correction that turned one of them into the best submission so far.

entry.title: The hard compounds are ordinary
entry.content:
What this post covers

The last post ended with a plan. If every model in my pool fails on the same compounds, the way forward is a model that has seen chemistry the others have not, which meant building a retrieved corpus of unlabelled near-neighbours of the blind set and pretraining the encoder on it. That is expensive, so before building it I checked whether the compounds I actually fail on are the kind of compounds such a corpus would contain.

They are not. This post covers that check (notebook 25), what the failures turned out to be instead (26), and the submission that came out of it (27). Every score below is a half-set measurement.1

Who the models get wrong

I defined three populations from the pooled out-of-fold predictions of all eleven configs, and froze the definitions to disk before computing a single chemical property, so the chemistry could not be fitted to the answer.2

  • Consensus-hard: worst decile by mean soft-threshold error across all eleven configs.
  • Consensus-easy: best decile by the same measure, as the contrast set.
  • Disagreement: worst decile by standard deviation of signed error across the eleven configs.

Each compound is held out once per repeat, so errors are averaged over a compound’s five repeats per config first. That separates a compound that gets mispredicted consistently by independently trained models from one that a single unlucky fold happened to miss.

The test that mattered is nearest-neighbour Tanimoto similarity to the training set, hard against easy. The expectation going in came from the activity-cliff literature, where the compounds that break structure-activity models are the ones whose near neighbours carry very different activity.3,4

Nearest-neighbour similarity to the training set for the hardest and easiest deciles, per isoform, medians dashed. The two distributions sit on top of each other everywhere.

Hard-set median similarity is 0.40, 0.44, 0.36 and 0.45 across CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4. The easy-set medians are 0.39, 0.44, 0.36 and 0.45. Rank-biserial effect sizes run 0.02 to 0.09 and none survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction on any isoform.

The compounds this pool fails on are exactly as well supported by nearest-neighbour structure as the compounds it gets right. A corpus built to cover structurally under-sampled territory would be aimed at a problem I do not have, so I did not build it. The check cost one read-only notebook and saved whatever the corpus would have cost.

What does separate them

Something had to distinguish the hard set, and on three isoforms it does. Hard compounds sit at higher measured pIC50, inside narrower credible intervals, with higher Crippen logP and lower FractionCSP3 than easy ones. That direction is consistent with the physicochemical profile repeatedly reported for CYP450 inhibitors, where lipophilicity and low sp3 character track inhibition across isoforms.5,6 CYP3A4 adds lower TPSA, higher heavy-atom count and a small enrichment of ring-free compounds (4 of the 6 acyclic compounds in its pool are hard, odds ratio 18.3, on an n small enough to say so out loud). CYP1A2 has nothing: no property tested separates its hard set by a material margin, so its difficulty is genuinely diffuse on this evidence.

Narrow intervals are partly mechanical, since the soft-threshold rule that defines hardness here is harder to satisfy when the tolerance band is tight. Potency is not mechanical, and it points somewhere specific.

The other half of the notebook asked whether being hard and being disputed are the same thing.

Mean soft-threshold error against the standard deviation of signed error across the eleven configs. Consensus-hard compounds (red) sit far to the right without sitting higher.

Spearman between difficulty and disagreement is 0.20, 0.25, 0.18 and 0.07 across the four isoforms, and the two sets overlap by only 11 to 19% of members. Being wrong and being disputed are largely independent populations here.

That is the compound-level counterpart to the error-correlation result from the last post. Model averaging works by cancelling the part of each member’s error that the others do not share.7,8 If the models disagreed about the compounds they get wrong, averaging would have something to cancel. They agree, confidently, on the same wrong answers.

The sign of the errors

Hard compounds being systematically more potent has an obvious candidate mechanism that nothing in this project had checked directly: a model whose predictions are compressed toward the mean will under-predict the potent tail hardest. Two prior findings are consistent with it. Under the scoring metric, under-prediction costs 1.65 to 2.79 times more than over-prediction of the same magnitude, and every submitted prediction distribution has a standard deviation below the training-label standard deviation on every isoform.

So I binned every compound by measured potency and looked at the sign.

Mean signed error (prediction minus true pIC50) by potency decile, all compounds. Red bars are under-predictions. One sign crossing per isoform, in the same place each time.

Textbook regression to the mean on all four isoforms. The lowest-potency decile is over-predicted by 1.11 to 1.88 pIC50 units, the trend is monotonic, and the highest-potency decile is under-predicted by 0.95 to 1.37. Between 64% and 93% of each hard set carries a negative signed error, all BH-significant against the easy set.

The compounds notebook 25 found hardest are the compounds sitting where the compression bites hardest. That is one mechanism, not two findings.

Is rho the right amount of shrinkage?

The calibration this project already deploys shrinks prediction spread by rho, the correlation between predictions and truth. That factor is provably optimal under squared error. The competition does not score squared error. Nobody had checked whether the two agree.

I swept a pure spread multiplier, holding each isoform’s prediction mean fixed, and scored every step through the unmodified evaluator. Spearman is asserted unchanged at three widely separated multipliers first, since scaling around a fixed centre cannot reorder anything and a failure there would mean the bug was mine.

Out-of-fold ST-RAE against a spread multiplier, mean held fixed. Dashed lines mark the raw predictions (s = 1) and the rho-shrinkage this project applies. The black dot is the ST-RAE optimum.

The optimum sits between rho and 1.0 on every isoform, closer to rho than to raw but never at it: 0.66 against rho 0.50 for CYP1A2, 0.82 against 0.65 for CYP2C9, 0.48 against 0.37 for CYP2D6, 0.91 against 0.75 for CYP3A4. The gap is 0.11 to 0.17 multiplier units every time.

Rho-shrinkage over-shrinks relative to what ST-RAE actually rewards, consistently, on all four. The absolute cost of using rho instead of the true optimum is small, 0.004 to 0.015 ST-RAE units, which is the same order as the headroom the offset sweep found. One honest asymmetry: CYP2C9’s stored rho was fitted on the capped Caruana ensemble9 rather than the model whose curve is plotted here, so its comparison point is not quite like the other three.

Sweeping offset and spread jointly showed the two corrections interact slightly on CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 (0.006, 0.003 and 0.008 ST-RAE units left on the table by optimising them separately) and are exactly separable on CYP2C9.

All of this is measured on out-of-fold data, and out-of-fold ST-RAE is known to be an unreliable guide for CYP2D6 specifically. Resampled cross-validation estimates carry no unbiased variance estimator to begin with,10 and here the problem is worse than variance: the recentring that took CYP2D6 from 1.1673 to 0.8299 on the real board scores 3.08 on the out-of-fold curve, roughly three times the raw baseline, because the two populations have different centres. A CYP2D6-only sweep against the solved blind population instead disagrees with the out-of-fold answer. I reported both side by side rather than averaging two answers to different questions.

Compression against the real board

Another entrant on this challenge, running under the name 450 nm, publishes a live operating dashboard of their own work, and it carries per-isoform evidence that their board ST-RAE is rank ordered by how compressed each submitted column was against the training-label spread.11 Their widest column, at 1.15 times training spread, scored 0.5087. Their narrowest, at 0.26 times, scored 1.794, which is worse than predicting a constant. It points the same way as SuperCowPowers’ independently reported observation that the true blind population is wider than the training data on every isoform,12 which means a column narrower than training spread is narrower still relative to the population it is actually scored against.

That is board evidence for the same phenomenon I had been measuring out-of-fold, and it implies a much larger effect. So I measured my own seven submitted files the same way, joined each column to its published score, and plotted all 28 points against their four.

Prediction spread relative to training-label spread against board ST-RAE. Coloured points are this project’s own seven submissions across four isoforms; crosses are the external entrant’s own four.

Pooled, the association is real and reasonably tight: Spearman −0.822, bootstrap 95% CI −0.888 to −0.662 over 28 points, in the same direction as the external claim.

Per isoform it mostly falls apart, and the naive p-values flatter it. CYP1A2’s rho of exactly −1.0 is an artefact: only 5 of its 7 submissions carry a distinct prediction column, so resampling from five clusters reproduces the same perfect order almost every draw and the bootstrap CI comes back degenerate at −1.0 to −1.0. CYP3A4’s CI runs −1.0 to 0.125, wide enough to contain zero. CYP2C9 and CYP2D6 are not significant at all. The only robust evidence in my own data is the pooled correlation.

The confound is worth stating plainly too. Those seven submissions differ in ensembling, in environment, and in three separate calibration mechanisms, not only in spread. Several columns’ ratios moved because a modelling decision changed, not because anything targeted spread. This is an observational association consistent with the compression hypothesis, not a demonstration of it.

My own current submission’s ratios: CYP3A4 0.933, CYP1A2 0.836, CYP2C9 0.817, and CYP2D6 at 0.608, 39% narrower than its training spread and the clear outlier of the four. CYP2D6 is also the most compressed and worst-scoring isoform in both sources.

The widening test

On cleanliness grounds CYP1A2 was the better candidate, since its column has been carried through byte-identical since the control run and has never been touched by a correction. I went with CYP2D6 anyway, because it is the only isoform whose compression is genuinely out of line with the rest and because four separate lines of evidence point the same way there: the ratio itself, the regression-to-the-mean signature, the asymmetric cost of under-prediction, and the external entrant’s own worst-scoring point.

One line of evidence points the other way, and I want it on the record rather than omitted. My own out-of-fold sweep says CYP2D6 wants more shrinkage, s = 0.48. I discounted that on a judgement, not a certainty: out-of-fold ST-RAE has already been shown to be invalid for this isoform, and if I had trusted it literally then the recentring that produced this project’s biggest real win would never have been attempted. This is a test of which evidence source is right for CYP2D6, not a confident correction.

The transform scales CYP2D6’s spread by 1.3971 about its own mean, landing the ratio at 0.85, in line with the other three isoforms and deliberately short of 1.0. The other three columns are carried over byte-identical.

The submitted CYP2D6 column (grey) and the widened one (red). The shaded band is the training-label spread, re-centred on the two histograms’ shared mean so it compares width only. Even after widening, the red distribution is narrower than the band.

Because a positive spread scale about a fixed mean is a strictly increasing map, it cannot reorder anything, which gives a prediction that can fail. Before submitting, I wrote down that CYP2D6’s board Spearman and Kendall should come back at exactly 0.4000 and 0.2747, unchanged, and that the other three isoforms should reproduce on every metric. If any of that moved, something other than the intended transform had happened and nothing else about the result could be trusted.

The result

Isoform Previous best Widened Change
CYP1A2 0.6954 0.6954 unchanged, as predicted
CYP2C9 0.5375 0.5375 unchanged, as predicted
CYP2D6 0.8299 0.7858 better
CYP3A4 0.4434 0.4434 unchanged, as predicted
Macro 0.6265 0.6155  

Best macro to date. CYP2D6’s Spearman and Kendall came back at 0.4000 and 0.2747, and the three untouched isoforms reproduced on every metric, which is the second time byte-identical resubmission has confirmed the board scores deterministically.

Both halves of the prediction held, which is what makes the improvement interpretable. The gain came from the spread of a column whose ordering never changed, on the isoform where the ordering was already known to be roughly right and the placement known to be wrong. Every move that has worked on this project so far has that shape.

Where this leaves things

A month ago I would have said the way to improve CYP2D6 was a better CYP2D6 model. Three separate corrections later, all of them arithmetic applied to predictions already made, it is at 0.7858 from a starting point of 1.1903, and not one of those corrections changed a single prediction’s rank.

The uncomfortable part is that the thing I keep correcting is the same thing every time. The models compress toward the mean, the metric punishes under-prediction harder than over-prediction, and the potent compounds pay for both. Recentring, then widening, are two ways of paying that back after the fact.

Which leaves the question the retrieved corpus was supposed to answer still open, and now with one route closed off by evidence rather than by cost. If the failures are ordinary compounds that every model agrees about and gets wrong in the same direction, the information that would fix them has to come from outside this dataset, and it has to be information about the compounds rather than about the chemical space around them. Multitask pretraining on external bioactivity data is the established route for exactly that shortage,13,14 with the standing caution that potency values aggregated across assays and laboratories carry substantial noise of their own.15
